decks.title: Hydrogen Chloride — Part 1: Preparation and physical properties
goals: Write the equation and describe the apparatus for preparing hydrogen chloride in the laboratory
Explain the choice of drying agent and method of collection
Describe experiments that show hydrogen chloride is heavier than air and very soluble in water
Explain how the inverted funnel prevents back suction when making hydrochloric acid

slides.heading: A gas that fumes in moist air
slides.body_md: Part 1 — Hydrogen chloride is a colourless gas with a sharp, choking smell. Open a jar of it in damp air and it forms **misty white fumes**: tiny droplets of hydrochloric acid.

visual.alt: Table of the physical properties of hydrogen chloride

slides.narration: Namaste! Hydrogen chloride is a colourless gas with a sharp, choking smell. When a jar of it is opened in damp air, it forms misty white fumes, because the gas dissolves in the water vapour to make tiny droplets of hydrochloric acid. In this part we make the gas, dry it, collect it, and look at how heavy and how soluble it is.

slides.heading: The reaction
slides.body_md:
Sodium chloride (rock salt) is heated gently with **concentrated sulphuric acid**, keeping the temperature **below 200 °C**. The acid gives its hydrogen to the chloride, forming **sodium hydrogensulphate** and hydrogen chloride.

Above 200 °C the reaction goes further to sodium sulphate, which is **avoided** (see the worked example).

visual.alt: Equation: sodium chloride plus sulphuric acid gives sodium hydrogensulphate plus hydrogen chloride
visual.caption: Laboratory preparation, below 200 °C

slides.narration: In the laboratory, sodium chloride is warmed with concentrated sulphuric acid. The temperature is kept below two hundred degrees Celsius. The products are sodium hydrogensulphate, which stays in the flask, and hydrogen chloride gas, which comes off. At higher temperatures a different salt forms, and we will see why that is a problem.

slides.heading: The apparatus
slides.body_md:
- **Flask:** sodium chloride + concentrated sulphuric acid added through a **thistle funnel**; gentle heat.
- **Wash bottle:** concentrated sulphuric acid **dries** the gas.
- **Gas jar:** kept **upright**; the gas enters at the bottom and pushes the air out — **upward displacement of air**.

slides.narration: Here is the apparatus. Concentrated sulphuric acid is added through a thistle funnel onto sodium chloride in a round bottomed flask, which is heated gently. The gas bubbles through a wash bottle of concentrated sulphuric acid to dry it. Then it is led to the bottom of an upright gas jar, where it pushes the lighter air out at the top.

slides.heading: Quick check: drying the gas
slides.body_md: Choose the drying agent for hydrogen chloride.
slides.narration: Quick check. The drying agent must absorb water but must not react with an acidic gas.

slides.heading: Drying and collecting
slides.body_md:
**Drying:** concentrated sulphuric acid absorbs water and does **not** react with hydrogen chloride. Quicklime and caustic soda are **bases** and would react with the gas.

**Collection:** by **upward displacement of air**, because the gas is **heavier than air**; never over water, because it is **extremely soluble**.

**Jar full?** A rod dipped in ammonia solution at the mouth gives **dense white fumes**; moist blue litmus turns **red**.

rows: Absorbs water; no reaction with HCl

visual.alt: Table of choices for drying and collecting hydrogen chloride with reasons

slides.narration: Concentrated sulphuric acid soaks up water but leaves hydrogen chloride alone, so it is the drying agent. Quicklime and caustic soda are bases, so they would react with the acidic gas. Hydrogen chloride is heavier than air, so it is collected in an upright jar, and it is far too soluble to collect over water. A rod dipped in ammonia solution shows when the jar is full.

slides.heading: Worked example: why stay below two hundred degrees?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A student heats the flask strongly, well above 200 °C. What changes, and why is this avoided?

**Step 1.** The reaction goes further: 2NaCl + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2HCl.

**Step 2.** Sodium sulphate forms a **hard crust** that sticks to the flask and is difficult to remove.

**Step 3.** The high temperature **wastes fuel** and may **crack the glass** flask.

rows: Hard crust; fuel wasted; glass may crack

visual.alt: Table comparing the products and problems below and above 200 degrees Celsius

slides.narration: If the flask is heated strongly, both hydrogen atoms of sulphuric acid are used and sodium sulphate is formed. This salt forms a hard crust that sticks to the flask and is very hard to clean out. The extra heat also wastes fuel and may crack the glass. So the mixture is warmed gently, below two hundred degrees Celsius.

slides.heading: Heavier than air
slides.body_md:
Relative molecular mass of HCl = 1 + 35.5 = 36.5, so its **vapour density is 18.25**. Air has an average vapour density of about **14.4**, so hydrogen chloride is **heavier than air**.

**Simple test:** tilt an open jar of the gas over an open jar of air as if pouring water. A rod dipped in ammonia solution then gives white fumes in the **lower** jar.

visual.alt: Table of vapour densities of air, hydrogen chloride and ammonia

slides.narration: The vapour density of a gas is half its relative molecular mass. For hydrogen chloride that is eighteen point two five, while air averages about fourteen point four. So hydrogen chloride is heavier than air. You can even pour it: tilt a jar of the gas over an empty jar, then a rod dipped in ammonia shows white fumes in the lower jar.

slides.heading: The fountain experiment
slides.body_md:
A dry flask of **dry hydrogen chloride** is clamped upside down with a jet tube dipping into water coloured with **blue litmus**. A few drops of water dissolve a large volume of gas, the **pressure inside falls**, and the outside air pressure pushes the water up as a **fountain**. The fountain turns **red**.

This shows the gas is **extremely soluble** and its solution is **acidic**.

As soon as a little water enters, it dissolves a huge amount of gas, so the pressure inside drops. The air pressing on the water outside pushes it up the tube in a fountain, and the blue colour turns red.

slides.heading: Quick check: the fountain
slides.body_md: Interpret the fountain experiment.
slides.narration: Quick check. Ask what the fountain shows, and what the change of colour shows.

slides.heading: Worked example: how much gas from rock salt?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** What mass of hydrogen chloride can be made from 23.4 g of sodium chloride? (Na = 23, Cl = 35.5, H = 1)

**Step 1.** NaCl + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HCl: one mole of NaCl gives one mole of HCl.

**Step 2.** NaCl = 58.5; moles = 23.4 ÷ 58.5 = 0.4.

**Step 3.** HCl = 36.5; mass = 0.4 × 36.5 = **14.6 g**.

visual.alt: Table showing that 0.4 mole of sodium chloride gives 0.4 mole, or 14.6 grams, of hydrogen chloride

slides.narration: From the equation, one mole of sodium chloride gives one mole of hydrogen chloride. The molar mass of sodium chloride is fifty eight point five, so twenty three point four grams is zero point four mole. Zero point four mole of hydrogen chloride, at thirty six point five grams per mole, has a mass of fourteen point six grams.

slides.heading: Making hydrochloric acid: the inverted funnel
slides.body_md:
If the delivery tube dipped straight into water, the gas would dissolve so fast that water could be **sucked back** into the hot flask (**back suction**), cracking it.

Instead the gas enters an **inverted funnel** whose **rim just dips** below the water. If water rises into the funnel, the level in the beaker falls below the rim, **air enters**, and the water falls back. The funnel also gives a **large surface** for absorption.

So the gas is led into an upside down funnel whose rim just touches the water. If water rushes up into the funnel, the level outside drops below the rim, air gets in, and the water simply falls back.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: NaCl + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HCl, heated below 200 °C.
Dried by concentrated sulphuric acid; collected by upward displacement of air.
Heavier than air (vapour density 18.25) and extremely soluble in water.
The fountain experiment shows high solubility and acidity (blue litmus turns red).
An inverted funnel prevents back suction when making hydrochloric acid.

visual.alt: Summary table of preparation, drying, collection and dissolving of hydrogen chloride

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Hydrogen chloride is made by warming sodium chloride with concentrated sulphuric acid below two hundred degrees Celsius. It is dried by concentrated sulphuric acid and collected by upward displacement of air. It is heavier than air and extremely soluble, as the fountain experiment shows, and it is dissolved in water through an inverted funnel.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Write the condition “below 200 °C” with the preparation equation.
For drying, say why the others fail: quicklime is basic and reacts.
Use “upward displacement of air” — not “downward”, which is for ammonia.
Explain the fountain with pressure: gas dissolves → pressure falls → air pushes water up.

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some tips. Always add the temperature condition to the preparation equation. When you name the drying agent, be ready to say why quicklime cannot be used. Remember that hydrogen chloride is collected by upward displacement of air. And explain the fountain experiment using pressure: the gas dissolves, the pressure falls, and the air outside pushes the water in.

decks.title: Hydrogen Chloride — Part 2: Chemical properties and tests
goals: Write balanced equations for hydrochloric acid with metals, oxides, hydroxides, carbonates, hydrogencarbonates, sulphides and sulphites
Describe the dense white fumes formed with ammonia
State the composition and use of aqua regia
Use silver nitrate and lead nitrate to identify hydrochloric acid and chlorides

slides.heading: Hydrochloric acid at work
slides.body_md: Part 2 — In water, hydrogen chloride ionises completely, so hydrochloric acid is a **strong acid**. It shows all the typical reactions of acids, plus some special ones of its own.

visual.alt: Table of the classes of substance that react with hydrochloric acid and the main products

slides.narration: When hydrogen chloride dissolves in water it ionises completely, so hydrochloric acid is a strong acid. It reacts with metals, bases, carbonates, sulphides and sulphites like any acid, and it also has special reactions, such as the white fumes it forms with ammonia and the white precipitates it gives with silver nitrate and lead nitrate.

slides.heading: With ammonia: dense white fumes
slides.body_md: Hydrogen chloride and ammonia gas combine directly to form tiny solid particles of **ammonium chloride**, seen as **dense white fumes**. This is used to **identify** either gas, and to check whether a jar of either gas is full.

visual.alt: Equation: ammonia plus hydrogen chloride gives ammonium chloride
visual.caption: Dense white fumes of ammonium chloride

slides.narration: When hydrogen chloride meets ammonia gas, the two combine at once to form ammonium chloride. This is a white solid, and it forms as a cloud of tiny particles, so we see dense white fumes. Because this reaction is so striking, a rod dipped in ammonia solution is used to test for hydrogen chloride, and a rod dipped in the acid is used to test for ammonia.

slides.heading: With active metals
slides.body_md: Metals **above hydrogen** in the activity series displace hydrogen: metal + hydrochloric acid → metal chloride + hydrogen. Iron gives **iron(II) chloride**. Metals **below hydrogen** (copper, silver, gold) do **not** react.

rows: Effervescence; gas burns with a pop

visual.alt: Table of the reactions of zinc, magnesium, iron and copper with dilute hydrochloric acid

slides.narration: Metals that are above hydrogen in the activity series push hydrogen out of the acid. Zinc and magnesium fizz and give hydrogen, which burns with a pop. Iron gives a pale green solution of iron two chloride. Copper, silver and gold are below hydrogen, so they do not react with dilute hydrochloric acid at all.

slides.heading: Quick check: acid and metal
slides.body_md: Predict the products of a metal with dilute hydrochloric acid.
slides.narration: Quick check. An active metal gives its chloride and one particular gas.

slides.heading: With oxides and hydroxides
slides.body_md: Metal oxides and hydroxides are **bases**: they **neutralise** hydrochloric acid to give a **salt and water** only.

rows: No visible change; heat given out

visual.alt: Table of the reactions of hydrochloric acid with copper oxide, sodium hydroxide and calcium hydroxide

slides.narration: Metal oxides and hydroxides are bases, so they neutralise the acid, giving a salt and water. Warm black copper oxide dissolves to give a blue green solution of copper chloride. Sodium hydroxide gives common salt and water, with heat given out. Calcium hydroxide gives calcium chloride and water.

slides.heading: With carbonates and hydrogencarbonates
slides.body_md: Carbonates and hydrogencarbonates give a chloride, water and **carbon dioxide**, seen as **brisk effervescence**. The gas turns **lime water milky**.

visual.alt: Table of equations for hydrochloric acid with calcium carbonate, sodium carbonate and sodium hydrogencarbonate

slides.narration: Carbonates and hydrogencarbonates fizz with hydrochloric acid, giving a chloride, water and carbon dioxide. Marble chips, washing soda and baking soda all behave this way. The gas is colourless and odourless, and it turns lime water milky. Notice that a carbonate needs two molecules of acid, while a hydrogencarbonate needs only one.

slides.heading: Worked example: gas from marble
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** What volume of carbon dioxide at STP is given off when 25 g of marble (calcium carbonate) reacts completely with dilute hydrochloric acid? (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16; molar volume 22.4 L)

**Step 1.** CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂: 1 mole CaCO₃ gives 1 mole CO₂.

**Step 2.** CaCO₃ = 40 + 12 + 48 = 100; moles = 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25.

**Step 3.** Volume = 0.25 × 22.4 = **5.6 L**.

visual.alt: Table of the steps from 25 grams of calcium carbonate to 5.6 litres of carbon dioxide

slides.narration: Write the balanced equation first: one mole of calcium carbonate gives one mole of carbon dioxide. The molar mass of calcium carbonate is one hundred, so twenty five grams is a quarter of a mole. A quarter of a mole of gas at standard temperature and pressure occupies a quarter of twenty two point four litres, which is five point six litres.

slides.heading: With sulphides and sulphites
slides.body_md: **Sulphides** give **hydrogen sulphide**, which smells of rotten eggs and turns lead acetate paper black. **Sulphites** give **sulphur dioxide**, which has a choking smell and turns orange acidified potassium dichromate **green**.

rows: Rotten-egg smell; lead acetate paper turns black
Choking smell; dichromate orange to green

visual.alt: Table of the reactions of hydrochloric acid with sulphides and sulphites and the tests for the gases

slides.narration: Sulphides react with the acid to give hydrogen sulphide, a gas that smells of rotten eggs and turns lead acetate paper black. Sulphites give sulphur dioxide, which has a choking smell and turns orange acidified potassium dichromate paper green. These two smells and tests help us identify unknown salts.

slides.heading: Worked example: which salt gave the gas?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to an unknown white salt. A gas with a choking smell is given off; it turns acidified potassium dichromate paper green but does not blacken lead acetate paper. Identify the gas and suggest the salt.

**Answer.** The gas is **sulphur dioxide** (choking smell, dichromate turns green). Lead acetate is not blackened, so it is **not** hydrogen sulphide. The salt is a **sulphite**, e.g. sodium sulphite: Na₂SO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + SO₂.

nodes.label: Lime water milky, no smell: CO₂ (carbonate)
Rotten eggs, lead acetate black: H₂S (sulphide)

visual.alt: Decision flow linking the gas given off with dilute hydrochloric acid to the type of substance

slides.narration: Use the properties of the gas. A choking smell points to sulphur dioxide or hydrogen sulphide. Acidified dichromate turning green fits sulphur dioxide, and the lead acetate paper staying unchanged rules out hydrogen sulphide. So the gas is sulphur dioxide, and the white salt must be a sulphite, such as sodium sulphite.

slides.heading: Precipitates with silver nitrate and lead nitrate
slides.body_md:
**Silver nitrate:** a **curdy white precipitate** of silver chloride, **insoluble in dilute nitric acid** but soluble in excess ammonium hydroxide.

**Lead nitrate:** a **white precipitate** of lead chloride, which **dissolves on heating** and reappears on cooling.

rows: Curdy white; insoluble in dil. HNO₃

slides.narration: Hydrochloric acid gives two important white precipitates. With silver nitrate solution it forms curdy white silver chloride, which does not dissolve in dilute nitric acid but does dissolve in excess ammonium hydroxide. With lead nitrate it forms white lead chloride, which dissolves when the mixture is heated and comes back on cooling.

slides.body_md: Recognise the silver chloride precipitate.
slides.narration: Quick check. Recall the colour of silver chloride and how it behaves in nitric acid.

slides.heading: Aqua regia
slides.body_md: **Aqua regia** (“royal water”) is a mixture of **three volumes of concentrated hydrochloric acid** and **one volume of concentrated nitric acid**. Nitric acid oxidises hydrochloric acid to **nascent chlorine**, which converts **gold and platinum** into soluble chlorides. It is used to dissolve these noble metals.

slides.narration: Aqua regia means royal water, because it dissolves gold, the king of metals. It is made by mixing three volumes of concentrated hydrochloric acid with one volume of concentrated nitric acid. The nitric acid oxidises the hydrochloric acid to give very reactive nascent chlorine, which turns gold and platinum into soluble chlorides.

slides.narration: To identify hydrogen chloride gas, hold moist blue litmus in it, which turns red, or a rod dipped in ammonia solution, which gives dense white fumes. To identify hydrochloric acid, add silver nitrate solution, which gives a curdy white precipitate that does not dissolve in dilute nitric acid. Lead nitrate gives a white precipitate that dissolves on heating.

sections.heading: 1. Laboratory preparation
sections.body_md:
**Reactants:** sodium chloride (rock salt) and **concentrated sulphuric acid**, heated gently **below 200 °C**.

- **Apparatus:** round-bottomed flask with a thistle funnel and delivery tube; wash bottle of concentrated sulphuric acid; upright gas jar.
- **Drying agent:** concentrated sulphuric acid (absorbs water, does not react). Quicklime and solid caustic soda are **not** used: they are bases and react with the gas.
- **Collection:** **upward displacement of air** (heavier than air); not over water (extremely soluble).
- **Jar full?** A rod dipped in ammonia solution gives dense white fumes; moist blue litmus turns red.
- **Why below 200 °C?** At a higher temperature sodium sulphate forms as a hard crust that sticks to the flask; fuel is wasted and the glass may crack.

key_terms.definition_md: Collection of a gas heavier than air in an upright jar: the gas enters at the bottom and pushes the air out at the top.
A substance that absorbs water vapour from a gas without reacting with the gas.

sections.heading: 2. Density and solubility; the fountain experiment
sections.body_md:
- **Density:** vapour density of HCl = 36.5 ÷ 2 = **18.25**, greater than that of air (about 14.4), so it is **heavier than air**. It can be "poured" from one jar into another.
- **Solubility:** extremely soluble in water; fumes in moist air.
- **Fountain experiment:** a dry flask of dry HCl, inverted, with a jet tube dipping into water containing blue litmus. A little water dissolves much gas, the pressure inside falls and atmospheric pressure drives water up as a **fountain**, which turns **red**. Shows **high solubility** and **acidic nature**.

key_terms.definition_md: Half the relative molecular mass of a gas; compares the mass of a volume of the gas with the same volume of hydrogen.
An experiment in which a very soluble gas dissolves in a little water, lowering the pressure so that water is forced into the flask as a fountain.

sections.heading: 4. Reactions of hydrochloric acid
sections.body_md:
- **With ammonia:** dense white fumes of ammonium chloride.
- **Active metals:** chloride + hydrogen (Zn, Mg, Fe → FeCl₂). Copper, silver, gold do not react.
- **Oxides and hydroxides:** salt + water (CuO gives a blue-green solution).
- **Carbonates and hydrogencarbonates:** chloride + water + CO₂ (effervescence; lime water milky).
- **Sulphides:** chloride + H₂S (rotten-egg smell; lead acetate paper black).
- **Sulphites:** chloride + water + SO₂ (choking smell; acidified potassium dichromate orange → green).

sections.heading: 5. Aqua regia
sections.body_md: **Aqua regia:** 3 volumes of concentrated HCl + 1 volume of concentrated HNO₃. Nitric acid oxidises hydrochloric acid to **nascent chlorine**, which converts **gold** and **platinum** into soluble chlorides. **Use:** dissolving noble metals (e.g. in testing and purifying gold).

sections.heading: 6. Precipitation reactions and tests
sections.body_md:
- **Silver nitrate:** AgNO₃ + HCl → AgCl + HNO₃; **curdy white** precipitate, insoluble in dilute HNO₃, soluble in excess NH₄OH.
- **Lead nitrate:** Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2HCl → PbCl₂ + 2HNO₃; white precipitate, **soluble in hot water**.

**Tests:** HCl gas — moist blue litmus turns red; dense white fumes with a rod dipped in ammonia solution. Hydrochloric acid — curdy white precipitate with silver nitrate solution (insoluble in dilute nitric acid).

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Leaving out "below 200 °C" from the preparation.
- Naming quicklime as the drying agent (it reacts with HCl).
- Saying HCl is collected by downward displacement (that is ammonia).
- Writing FeCl₃ for iron with dilute HCl (it is FeCl₂).
- Reversing the 3 : 1 ratio of aqua regia.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Equations (1 mark each): correct formulae, balanced, with conditions where asked.
- Observations (1 mark): colour, smell, effervescence or precipitate, stated clearly.
- Fountain experiment: set-up, reason (pressure) and the colour change.

options.text_md: heavier than air and very soluble in water

questions.solution_md: Equation with condition.

questions.stem_md: Why is quicklime not used to dry hydrogen chloride gas?

answer.model_answer_md: Quicklime is a basic oxide and reacts with the acidic gas: CaO + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O.

questions.solution_md: It reacts with HCl.

questions.stem_md: Explain why hydrogen chloride is (a) collected by upward displacement of air and (b) never collected over water.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) It is heavier than air (vapour density 18.25 against about 14.4 for air), so it sinks to the bottom of the upright jar and pushes the air out. (b) It is extremely soluble in water, so it would dissolve instead of collecting.

questions.solution_md: Density; solubility.

questions.stem_md: In the laboratory preparation of hydrogen chloride, the flask is heated gently and kept below 200 °C. Give two reasons why a higher temperature is avoided.

answer.model_answer_md: Above 200 °C the reaction goes further, 2NaCl + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2HCl, and (1) the sodium sulphate forms a hard crust that sticks to the flask and is difficult to remove; (2) the glass flask may crack, and more fuel is wasted.

questions.solution_md: Crust of sodium sulphate; cracking and fuel.

questions.stem_md: What mass of sodium chloride, in grams, is needed to prepare 7.3 g of hydrogen chloride by the reaction NaCl + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HCl? (Na = 23, Cl = 35.5, H = 1)
questions.solution_md: Molar masses: NaCl $= 23 + 35.5 = 58.5$; HCl $= 1 + 35.5 = 36.5$. One mole of NaCl gives one mole of HCl, so mass of NaCl $= \dfrac{58.5}{36.5} \times 7.3 = 11.7$, that is 11.7 g.

is a neutral gas
does not dissolve in water
is heavier than air

the flask is heated, so the gas expands
water is lighter than hydrogen chloride and floats upwards

questions.stem_md: Calculate the vapour density of hydrogen chloride. (H = 1, Cl = 35.5)
questions.solution_md: Relative molecular mass of HCl $= 1 + 35.5 = 36.5$. Vapour density $= \dfrac{36.5}{2} = 18.25$.

questions.stem_md: In the fountain experiment with hydrogen chloride: (a) why must the flask and the gas be completely dry? (b) explain why the water rises into the flask as a fountain; (c) name the two properties of hydrogen chloride shown by the experiment.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) If water were present, some gas would dissolve before the experiment and the pressure difference would be too small for a good fountain. (b) The first drops of water dissolve so much gas that the pressure inside the flask falls far below atmospheric pressure; the outside air pressure on the trough pushes water up the jet. (c) It is highly soluble in water, and its solution is acidic (turns blue litmus red).

options.text_md: dries the gas before it dissolves

options.text_md: Water is sucked back into the generating flask
Air enters the funnel, the pressure is equalised and the water inside falls back into the beaker
The gas stops dissolving permanently

questions.stem_md: Explain how the inverted funnel arrangement prevents back suction when hydrogen chloride is dissolved in water.

answer.model_answer_md: The rim of the inverted funnel just touches the water. If the gas dissolves fast and water rises into the funnel, the water level in the beaker falls below the rim; air then enters the funnel, the pressure is equalised and the water drops back. So water is never sucked back into the generating flask.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write the balanced equation for the laboratory preparation of hydrogen chloride from sodium chloride, and state the temperature condition. [2]

(b) Name the drying agent used, and give a reason why quicklime is not used. [2]

(c) Name the method of collecting the gas, give a reason for it, and state how you would know that the gas jar is full. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) NaCl + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HCl; the mixture is heated below 200 °C.

(b) Concentrated sulphuric acid. Quicklime is basic and reacts with hydrogen chloride (CaO + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O).

(c) Upward displacement of air, because the gas is heavier than air (and too soluble to collect over water). A rod dipped in ammonia solution held at the mouth gives dense white fumes (or moist blue litmus turns red).

(d) The gas is led into an inverted funnel whose rim just dips below the water in a beaker. If water rises into the funnel, the level in the beaker falls below the rim, air enters and the water falls back, so it cannot be sucked into the generating flask. The funnel also gives a large surface for absorption.

questions.solution_md: Equation and condition; drying agent; collection and test; inverted funnel.

(b) Tilt an open jar of hydrogen chloride over an open jar of air, as if pouring a liquid; a rod dipped in ammonia solution held in the lower jar then gives dense white fumes.

A few drops of water entering dissolve much gas, the pressure inside falls, and atmospheric pressure forces the water up the tube as a fountain; the blue litmus turns red.

(d) (i) Misty white fumes. (ii) The gas dissolves in the water vapour of the air, forming tiny droplets of hydrochloric acid. (iii) Hydrogen chloride is very soluble in water.

(b) Write balanced equations for the reactions of dilute hydrochloric acid with (i) calcium carbonate and (ii) sodium hydrogencarbonate. [2]

(d) (i) Explain why silver does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid. (ii) Calculate the volume of hydrogen at STP given off when 3.25 g of zinc reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid. (Zn = 65; molar volume 22.4 L) [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. (ii) Fe + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂.

(b) (i) CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. (ii) NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂.

(c) Na₂SO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + SO₂. Sulphur dioxide turns orange acidified potassium dichromate paper green (or decolourises acidified potassium permanganate).

(d) (i) Silver is below hydrogen in the activity series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from the acid. (ii) One mole of zinc gives one mole of hydrogen. Moles of zinc $= \dfrac{3.25}{65} = 0.05$; volume of hydrogen $= 0.05 \times 22.4 = 1.12$, that is 1.12 L.

Four test tubes, A, B, C and D, contain sodium carbonate, iron(II) sulphide, zinc granules and sodium sulphite, not in that order. Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to each.

(a) The gas from A burns with a pop. Identify A and write the equation. [2]

(b) The gas from B turns lime water milky but has no smell. Identify B and write the equation. [2]

(c) C and D both give gases with a smell. The gas from C turns lead acetate paper black; the gas from D turns acidified potassium dichromate green but not lead acetate paper. Identify C and D and name both gases. [3]

(d) Silver nitrate solution is added to the liquid left in B after the reaction. State the observation, write the equation for it, and explain why dilute nitric acid is added before the silver nitrate in such tests. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A is zinc: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂.

(b) B is sodium carbonate: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂.

(c) C is iron(II) sulphide, giving hydrogen sulphide; D is sodium sulphite, giving sulphur dioxide.

(d) A curdy white precipitate: NaCl + AgNO₃ → AgCl + NaNO₃. Dilute nitric acid removes carbonate (and sulphite) ions, which would otherwise also give a white precipitate with silver nitrate; silver chloride alone stays undissolved in it.
